Subject: Access options for Redwood Private — short summary request

Mina,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. Security asked me to get a concise write-up comparing three ways to connect our VPC to Redwood Private for the pilot: VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site VPN to the customer-managed gateway. They want the tradeoffs focused specifically on:

- Data plane isolation and attacker surface area
- Authentication and traffic flow (IP vs. endpoint)
- Operational overhead during patching/failover
- Observability (tracing, source IP preservation)
- What we can commit to in a SOC/audit timeline for the PoC

If you have a one-page matrix and a recommended default for a regulated banking PoC, that would help move us to the mutual action plan.

Appreciate it —
Liam

Liam —

Quick ack and attaching a one-page matrix + a draft network diagram. High-level recommendation up front: for the pilot we typically recommend PrivateLink (interface endpoint) when customers need strong tenant isolation and limited blast radius, but there are cases where peering or S2S is preferable. Notes below; full detail in the attachment.

Attachment: redwood-privatedeploy-onramp-playbook.pdf (one-pager + reference links)
Attachment: aegis_mvp_network_diagram.vsdx (sketch of three options)

TL;DR (pilot):
- Default: PrivateLink (interface endpoint) — minimizes public IP exposure, explicit endpoint-managed ACLs, preserves per-connection auth, and aligns well with our audit controls.
- If you need direct source IP preservation for legacy appliances or whitelisting at your end, use VPC peering — but peering increases tenant visibility and routing complexity.
- Use site-to-site VPN only if you require on-prem-only access (no cloud VPC) or need policy-enforced WAN controls; expect higher latency and operational overhead.

I'll loop in Kimberly and Karthik for the SOC-2/audit timeline implications and to call out any service limits. If you want, we can run a short PoC with PrivateLink and keep peering as a fallback.

Next steps:
1) Review the one-pager and diagram (attached).
2) Approve a 2-week PoC scope (we'll push a PoC mutual-action-plan).
3) If approved, we'll schedule a technical deep-dive with your network team (30–45m).

Thanks,
Mina

Liam / Mina —

Additions from the infra/security perspective (short bullets that map to the matrix):

- Authentication / identity: PrivateLink integrates with our mTLS front door per-customer certs for the control plane and supports token-based auth for per-request validation. Peering relies on network-level isolation and any app-layer auth you already have; we recommend enforcing mutual TLS at the app layer in that case.

- IP preservation & observability: Peering preserves source IP which helps with third-party appliances and SIEM correlation. PrivateLink will show traffic coming from the interface endpoint IPs (we surface source metadata in the X-Redwood-Source header) — we provide tokenized request IDs and tracing hooks back to your tracing system. VPN terminates at your edge, and NAT behavior depends on appliance config.

- Blast radius & lateral movement: PrivateLink gives the smallest datacenter-side surface area — only our endpoint service is addressable from your VPC. Peering broadens the routable space; we need strict prefix filters. VPN exposes the on-prem network depending on BGP/routing.

- Operational overhead: VPNs require certificate/key rotation and customer gateway maintenance, plus potential MTU/path MTU issues. Peering needs route table hygiene and coordination for prefix changes. PrivateLink is lower-touch operationally but requires interface endpoint lifecycle ops on customer side.

- Backup/failover: For high-availability, we recommend dual-path: primary PrivateLink + secondary S2S (or cross-region PrivateLink) for regulated traffic. Failover automation is part of our recommended PoC runbook (see attached MAP).

I'll draft a short SOC evidence checklist (logs, flow logs, cert rotation notes) after the PoC scope is locked.

-Kim

Liam / Carlos / team —

Attached: mutual-action-plan.xlsx (first draft) — includes a 3-week PoC schedule, roles, and an evidence checklist mapped to SOC 2 items (logs, KV cache retention, access logs, cert rotation cadence).

Answers inline to your questions: 
1) Sample flow logs: attached PDF excerpt in the playbook shows X-Redwood-Source + request-id examples from a recent PrivateLink PoC (we redact tokens). We can run a masked extract for your environment during the PoC.

2) Peering guardrails: when peering is used we enforce strict prefix ACLs and an automated route-advertisement policy that only allows our service subnets; any route change requires a signed change request and we can push change notifications to your netops Slack channel. We also enable RPKI-origin validation where supported and provide a weekly routing report during the PoC.

Proposed schedule (from MAP):
- Week 0: Kick, onboard network contacts, exchange certs and subnets
- Week 1: PrivateLink provisioning + basic smoke tests (auth + gen/response)
- Week 2: Observability run (flow logs, tracing), failover rehearsal to VPN fallback
- Week 3: Evidence collection + wrap + sign-off criteria

If that looks good, we'll send a calendar invite for the kickoff and a short tech agenda (30m) for next Tuesday.

Thanks — we'll also attach the PoC SOW if procurement needs it.

Best,
Mina
